summaries.example: Imagine measuring a desk with a ruler. You line up the ruler, look at the marks, and count the distance. Now imagine measuring the distance to the Moon. A ruler will not work, so scientists use a different method involving light and time. Operationalism asks us to notice that changing the method can change what the measurement means.
summaries.summary: Operationalism is the idea that we understand a scientific concept by looking at the operations used with it. An operation is an action, such as lining up a ruler, counting, observing, or calculating. P. W. Bridgman used length as an important example. We can measure a nearby object with a ruler, but we need other methods for very large distances, and different methods may be needed for very tiny things. Bridgman warned that we should not automatically assume that one concept works in exactly the same way everywhere. Later philosophers criticized a very strong version of operationalism. They argued that a measurement method does not give the whole meaning of a concept, and that useful scientific ideas may sometimes be connected to measurements indirectly. The entry also explains a more helpful lesson: studying what scientists do can make scientific practice clearer, while reminding us that nature can be complicated and measurements are never perfectly exact.
key_ideas: We should pay attention to the actual actions used to measure things.
The same word may be used in different situations even when different measuring methods are needed.
A measuring method may not work everywhere.
Operational thinking can help scientists notice confusion before it causes problems.
Some philosophers thought operationalism was too strict because measurements do not contain every part of an idea’s meaning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Operational thinking teaches us to slow down and ask, “How do we know this?” It helps scientists explain their methods and notice when an idea is being used outside the situation where it was first tested. It also prevents us from believing that a number is meaningful just because we can write it down. At the same time, the criticisms remind us that science needs more than simple measuring rules: theories, comparisons, and careful reasoning can also matter.

important_terms.definition: A way of thinking about a concept by asking what actions or measurements are used to apply it.
A careful action used to find out or measure something, such as lining up a ruler or counting marks.
A rule or method that explains how a scientific idea will be measured or used.
A feature or idea that scientists try to study, such as length, time, or temperature.

questions_to_think_about: Would measuring the length of a pencil and the distance to a faraway star require the same action?
Can a measuring tool tell us everything about an idea?
What might go wrong if we use a familiar word in a brand-new situation?

summaries.example: Suppose a theory assigns a length to an electron by combining equations with measurements made at larger scales. If the length used in the equations cannot be measured independently at the tiny scale, then testing the theory may become circular: the theory helps define the measurement, while the supposed measurement is then used to test the theory. Bridgman’s operational analysis exposes this loss of independent empirical content, even though critics argue that theoretical concepts can still be scientifically valuable when they connect several measurable results.
summaries.summary: Operationalism developed from P. W. Bridgman’s reflections on experimental practice. Its central impulse is to examine a concept through the operations by which scientists determine, apply, or test it. Bridgman’s discussion of length shows why this matters: a ruler is suitable for some ordinary objects, while astronomical distances require procedures involving light, time, and inference. At very small or very large scales, familiar measurement operations may cease to apply, so extending a concept without examining the new procedures can create conceptual confusion. Bridgman sometimes expressed an extreme view in which a concept meant no more than its associated operations. The entry explains why that view failed as a general theory of meaning. Measurements capture only some aspects of meaning, and science often needs theoretical concepts whose connections to observation are indirect. Further problems concern what counts as an operation and whether operations are essentially public laboratory procedures or also involve private acts of judgment and understanding. Critics such as Hempel feared that treating different procedures as different concepts would destroy the systematic unity of science. The entry nevertheless identifies a more modest and promising legacy. Operational analysis can be understood as a practice-oriented method that studies scientific activities, regulates the extension of concepts into new domains, and seeks to preserve or increase empirical content. It also reveals that both nature and scientific practice may be too complex for a single perfectly unified description.
key_ideas: Bridgman’s original reflections arose from experimental problems, especially the limits of measurement under unfamiliar conditions.
Length illustrates that one word can cover procedures used in very different domains, from rulers to methods involving light and complex inference.
A strong reduction of meaning to operations is inadequate: operational definitions do not exhaust meaning, and not every useful concept has a direct operational definition.
Operations are not limited to laboratory instrument use; they can include mental, verbal, computational, and paper-and-pencil activities.
Critics worried that multiplying concepts whenever procedures differ would fragment science and undermine its search for systematic unity.

A revised operationalism can function as a method for extending concepts carefully, increasing empirical content, and analyzing scientific practice without treating operations as infallible foundations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Operationalism matters because it focuses attention on the connection between concepts and scientific activity. It encourages researchers to state how a concept is being used, what evidence supports it, and whether a procedure has been extended beyond its tested range. Its critics establish an equally important limit: methods do not automatically provide a complete meaning, and theory cannot always be reduced to direct measurement. In its revised form, operational analysis is less a rigid doctrine than a disciplined strategy for making concepts clearer, more testable, and more responsibly connected across different domains.

important_terms.definition: A view associated with Bridgman that analyzes concepts through the activities, measurements, calculations, and other procedures connected with them.
An activity or procedure through which a concept is applied, tested, measured, or made clearer; it may be instrumental, mental, verbal, or paper-and-pencil.
A specification of the procedure used to identify or measure a concept in a particular setting.
The content of a theory that can be connected with observations, tests, or possible empirical failures.
The idea that one concept can remain connected across different settings when different procedures produce appropriately consistent results and other links support the connection.
A scientific idea that may not be directly measurable but can connect or organize several operationally meaningful concepts.
The philosophical study of science in terms of activities, actions, and events rather than only objects, statements, or theories.

questions_to_think_about: When two procedures give convergent results, what justifies treating them as measuring one concept rather than two related concepts?
Can a theoretical concept be scientifically useful if it lacks a direct operational definition? What kinds of indirect links might support it?
Does operational analysis protect science from untested conceptual extensions, or can it make scientific concepts unnecessarily fragmented?
Why might an operation include calculation or judgment rather than only physical manipulation of an instrument?
What does the limited precision of every measurement imply about the hope for complete certainty in science?

summaries.example: Think about the word “temperature.” A kitchen thermometer works in an ordinary range, but it may fail in a very hot kiln. A scientist might need another method based on how a material changes when heated. If the new method overlaps with the old one and gives results that fit together, we may keep using the same word. Operationalism says we should check those links instead of assuming the word automatically keeps exactly the same meaning.
summaries.summary: Operationalism is a philosophical approach that connects scientific concepts with the operations used to investigate them. P. W. Bridgman developed this approach while thinking about experimental physics. In high-pressure experiments, ordinary measuring instruments could fail, forcing scientists to create new ways to determine pressure. He used length as a model case: a ruler can measure familiar objects, but other procedures are needed for distances to the Moon, stars, or very small particles. This suggests that a concept may not work in exactly the same way in every setting. Bridgman urged scientists to examine the details of their procedures rather than quietly carrying old assumptions into new areas. The approach became controversial when it was treated as a complete theory of meaning. Critics argued that an operational definition gives only one part of a concept’s meaning and that some important scientific concepts are theoretical or connected to evidence indirectly. They also questioned what counts as an operation. It might involve instruments, but it can also involve calculations, language, counting, and judgment. Another disagreement concerned whether scientific operations must be public and objective. Bridgman emphasized the scientist’s own acts of understanding, while other operationists valued publicly checkable procedures. The entry presents a more moderate lesson that remains useful: operations can help scientists extend concepts carefully, increase a theory’s contact with evidence, and analyze scientific work as a series of activities. This lesson does not require believing that every concept is nothing more than a measurement procedure.
key_ideas: Bridgman developed operational analysis from questions raised by doing experiments, especially when old instruments stopped working.
Different situations may require different procedures for what we casually call the same thing.
Operational definitions can make research more precise, but they do not necessarily give the entire meaning of a concept.
Not every useful scientific concept must be directly measurable; some concepts work through indirect theoretical connections.
Critics worried that operationalism could split science into too many separate concepts and weaken its search for a unified explanation.
A less extreme version of operationalism can help scientists extend ideas carefully and study science as something people do.
summaries.why_it_matters: Operationalism matters because it asks scientists to connect words and theories with actual investigative practices. That can reveal when a familiar concept is being used in a new setting without enough evidence. It also helps researchers design clearer experiments and distinguish direct measurements from indirect inferences. The objections are just as valuable: science cannot be reduced to a list of procedures, because concepts can have wider meanings and theories can organize evidence in complex ways. Together, the idea and its criticisms encourage both precision and caution.

important_terms.definition: The view that the meaning of a scientific idea is closely connected to the actions and procedures used to measure or investigate it.
A procedure carried out to investigate or measure something, including using tools, counting, calculating, or making judgments.
A stated procedure for deciding how a concept will be identified or measured in a particular case.
An idea used by science to organize or describe observations, such as length, time, force, or temperature.
The ability of a scientific idea or theory to make contact with observations and tests.
The condition in which different methods give results that agree within the range where both methods can be used.

questions_to_think_about: If two thermometers use different methods, what reasons might support calling both measurements “temperature”?
Why might a theory include ideas that cannot be measured directly?
Are mental acts such as counting or judging part of a scientific operation?
How could insisting on a clear procedure improve a psychology experiment?
Why might scientists need both careful measurements and broader theories?
